reverse_outline.summary: Key points: Corvane is invented, its five stages each had a sensible structure, and its eight incidents are matched to failure patterns
Corvane is a fictional company whose facts are kept in one ledger so every chapter means the same thing by it
The page's claim: each structure was reasonable when built and incidents came where growth moved the shortage / The five steps in which the page presents the company
What Corvane sells: scheduling software for field-service firms, in three parts (web, mobile, integrations)
Why this product suits the book: a gap between teams shows up as a fault the customer sees
The three capacities used to read each stage: attention, judgment, verification
Ten years divide into five stages, each ending in a named incident (timeline figure)
How to read the full table of the five stages
Stage 1: one team at 12 people, and every decision waiting for the CTO (the Founder Queue)
Stage 2: four teams at 50 people, nobody holding the whole product, and the same scheduling rule built twice, two times over (Two Calendars, Second Calendar)
Stage 3: engineers doubled at 180 people, but changes waited on a five-person platform team to be released (the Launch Queue)
Stage 4: groups and planning at 500 people put deciders far from the facts (Nine-Week Plan, Tuesday Reorg)
Stage 5: coding agents at 1,100 people make writing cheap, reviews pile up, and hiring itself comes into question (Review Wall, Hiring Question)
The shape common to all five stages: a structure right for its problem and wrong once the shortage moved
Introduces the table of the seven named people and their roles
The named people are roles, not culprits; no incident is explained by a person failing
Team names by stage, so a team name tells you when a scene happens

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 26 aligned units match the controlling idea of their spec paragraph (p01-p26); the stage 3 summary names only the Launch Queue, but the unit itself carries the even split, the forty-one features and the open question p10 asks for.
The only unit marked two_ideas is Introduction ¶2 (claim plus roadmap); spec p02 asks for exactly that pair, so it holds no idea the spec did not ask for.
Every unit serves the supporting claim its section declares: company S1, five stages S2, cast S3 (team names serve the lookup, S5), incidents S4, usage S5; no orphan unit.

Figure 1 has a caption and a lead-in; each of the four tables is introduced and its columns or caveats explained; the stage 3 and stage 5 figures are interpreted in the text ('About two of the 19 days go into writing the change. The rest is waiting'). Note: the stage 3 product-and-tech cell gives 95, 11 and 7 and no total, unlike the other rows.

Every declared transition_in is expressed at its boundary, and the hand-off to Part I is an elaboration ('What plain words do not yet give is the reason'). Two are carried by format more than by a sentence: the five-stages section opens on the capacities and takes its time relationship from the heading, and stage 5 opens on the acquisition with the time relationship in its dated lead, without carrying over 'groups and plans'.

results.quote: Core is dissolved when the eleven teams are formed in 2023, and its work is divided among them.
results.finding: Stage 2 gave the rule engine 'one home', the Core team, and said the failure does not come back; the cast section then dissolves Core a year later and the page never says who owns the rule engine afterwards. Both readers went back to stages 2 and 3 and were left unsure. The spec's p16 does not ask for Core's dissolution; the draft added a fact that reopens the stage 2 fix.

results.finding: The introduction opens with a direct statement tied to the previous page, declares the fiction, states a disputable claim and gives the roadmap; no placeholder, restated question, definition, sweeping history or book-report opening.
The conclusion does not merely restate, introduce a new argument, apologize or end on a quotation; the 150-to-300 band in ¶4 is new but is the callback the spec asks for, recorded under flow.

¶4 states the synthesis (claim, patterns and Corvane as one instrument) and ¶5 the so-what: the reader can say what went wrong at each size in plain words and is ready for the vocabulary that explains why; the takeaway question is asked.

The hiring wave the book's introduction opened with is placed as 'stage 3 of five, at 180 people', with the stage before explaining the teams and the stage after the plans, as the spec's callback declares.
The intro reader predicted all five roadmap promises in order (product, five stages with sizes, cast, incidents matched to patterns, usage table) and the kind of evidence (invented illustration).

The cold reader listed the five stages in order with 12, 50, 180, 500 and about 1,100 people and the named incident of each, from the stage table alone. The criterion's expected answer says 'near 150' for stage 3 while the spec's own table (p07) fixes 180; the answer is accepted as near, and the expected text should be aligned with the table.

The first paragraph says 'Corvane is fictional', that it is not a disguised portrait of a real company, and that every number is an illustration, never a measurement; the callout, the conclusion and Sources repeat it, and no figure on the page is presented as data about a real company.
